(1) extremely high velocity (EHVs) wings are seen on CO J=3−2 lines toward 8 out of the 10 sources observed, and (2) the EHV wings have full widths of 70–140 km s − 1 and peak velocities of 20–50 km s − 2.
the EHV outflows are optically thin, have a wide range of velocities and spatial distributions, and have a wide range in their physical properties.
the CO emission from the outflows is optically thick and that there are two components of CO outflow emission with different morphologies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of high and extremely high velocity CO gas in star-forming regions.
the study of the properties of the molecular outflows in a sample of high-mass young stellar objects.
the following: (1) the nature of the outflowing gas, (2) the origin of the extremely high-velocity wings, and (3) the relationship between the outflows and the ambient molecular clouds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the extremely high velocity wings are optically thin.
the EHV wings are not due to a foreground cloud.
the EHV gas is associated with the outflow and is not simply the result of a projection effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EHV wings are ubiquitous in massive star-forming regions and may represent a generic feature of the massive star formation process.
the CO EHV outflows are not necessarily bipolar, and they are not necessarily associated with the high-velocity outflow components.
